title: Dancing Queens
reviewNotes: Three branches check two pictured five-piece pawn endings: Kd6 at 157s wins, Ke7 at 33s loses. Independent representative continuations show capture of c5, coordinated pawn advances and king march, capture of the outside pawn’s promoted queen, and final promotion; earlier-exchange comparison loses c4. Missing the immediate c5 capture also loses. The nine-piece queen dances and source Kd6 tempo claim remain outside this exact reconstruction.
transcript: White promotes to a new queen, but wait, so does black. So, is this going to be a draw? Not exactly. White could try to give a check, induce the queen to cover the king, and then after this other check, force a trade, and push the king in front of his own pawn, meaning that white is going to promote faster. But actually, incredibly, this position is a draw after king to c2, because there is no way to check this black king directly. And if you try to be tricky, and for example, play queen to g8, and meet [music] the queen promotion with this check and exchange, actually, it is black that is going to win the game, thanks to this passed pawn that is going to distract the white king, and then the black king is going to collect this pawn, and very easily promote it. So, none of this can work. And after both sides decide to get a new queen, they have to try to get the next one as fast as possible. Black pushes his pawn, too. And now, on queen to a8, queen a2 can be met with another promotion to a new [music] queen, because, of course, if black decides to capture this queen, after we recapture with a check, the king is forced in front of the pawn, and this time, we are the only ones with a queen on the board, and we are going to use it to win this end game, for example, like this. But black is not that naive, and instead of capturing that queen on a8, he decides to promote his other pawn to another queen, queen to h8, check. Now, this queen is pinned by our other queen, so the only move available is queen one to b2. And now, white [music] follows up with queen to h1, check. And again, this time, this queen is pinned to the king, so the only move is queen a to b1. But now, we have freed up this square, so that we can play queen eight to a8, check. And this time, this queen is the pinned one, so we force queen two to a2. And now, we have created this very weird construction where both queens are pinned and our two queens are communicating across the board. But if we give another check, we are just going to repeat moves. And if we trade the queens, we are [music] actually going to end in that lost end game where black is going to use this pawn as a destruction. So how can white possibly be winning in this position? You see, white has the very elegant [music] and majestic king to D6. Between all of these chaos between these extremely powerful pieces, [music] the king starts to make the difference with only one little step. Because you see, these queens are pinned anyway. And if black ever decides to trade them, actually this time, because of this little step that we took with the king, this king and pawn end game is won [music] for white. The king is closing off to run to stop the black pawn. And whenever the black king tries to chase the white pawn, well, the white pawn can just run away, which means that white is going to stop this promotion and then push his own pawn to victory.
